title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: Before 8000 BC · Bone Grease, Fat Lamps, the First Pots and the Hunter’s Fat

entries.label: Fat as the hunter’s target, and perhaps a reason to domesticate
entries.loc: The Aleutians and the American Plains
entries.hint: Kiple notes that selection for the fattest animals is documented in the preference of prehistoric Aleut hunters for sea lions, the largest and fattiest sea mammals, and in the bison remains from archaeological sites, which show selection of the fattest individuals. Domestic animals store more fatty tissue than their wild ancestors, which may have been a further incentive to keep them.
entries.note: CONTEXT (an argument in an encyclopedia chapter): Kiple (2000) the introduction on food and subsistence (PDF pp.93–95), citing Yesner 1988, Denniston 1972 and Armitage 1986. The date is a placeholder for the end of the Ice Age; the Aleut and bison remains are not dated in the passage.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Marrow, fish in the first pots, and the wild olive

entries.label: Wild olive stones heaped in Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites
entries.hint: Hints of the first human uses of the wild olive, the oleaster, are scattered through the Palaeolithic and Neolithic layers across the Mediterranean: from Spain and the French Riviera to North Africa, the Greek islands and Israel, archaeologists have found heaps of oleaster pits that suggest the fruit was being collected. These show gathering, not pressing; the evidence for a cultivated tree begins in the Chalcolithic Levant.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; no sites or dates named): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the opening chapter. The range is the ‘Paleolithic and Neolithic’ of his sentence, not a dating. See fats-8000bc-1200bc::ec2 for the domesticated olive.

entries.label: Japan’s Incipient Jōmon cooks boil fish and sea animals in the world’s earliest pots
entries.hint: Lipids recovered from charred deposits on Incipient Jōmon pottery of about 15,000 to 11,800 years ago show that most of the pots were used to process freshwater and marine organisms: of 101 deposits across Japan’s main islands, isotope values point to high-trophic-level aquatic food. The authors suggest that productive waters may have prompted the investment in pottery. A later study of about 800 vessels links early pottery with intensified fishing, first of salmon and then of a wider range including shellfish and marine mammals.
entries.note: SECONDARY (abstracts and university news found by web search; papers not read): Craig et al., ‘Earliest evidence for the use of pottery’, Nature 496 (2013) pp.351–354; University of York news of 2018 on about 800 vessels. Residues show aquatic foods were cooked; they do not isolate marine fat as such.

entries.label: Hunters crack bones for marrow and boil out grease: akutuk and pemmican
entries.loc: The Arctic and the Great Plains, recorded practice
entries.hint: Northern hunting peoples’ recorded practice shows what an early fat economy looked like. Caribou are lean except for fat round the viscera, under the skin and in the marrow; the ends of the long bones are smashed for marrow, and the fragments boiled to make ‘bone juice’. Inuit informants prized marrow for its low-melting-point oleic acid. Marrow and back-fat go into akutuk, ‘Eskimo ice cream’, with berries and snow; on the Plains, hot liquid marrowfat poured over pulverised jerky and sealed in a hide sack was pemmican, from Cree pimikân, grease.
entries.note: CONTEXT (recorded practice of recent peoples, not a Palaeolithic find): Kiple (2000) the caribou-hunting chapter (PDF p.521, after Binford 1978 and Spiess 1979) and the pemmican passage in the cattle chapter (PDF p.488). The date is a placeholder for the end of the Ice Age; the antiquity of the method is shown only by sites such as te1.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Rendering bone grease and burning fat for light

entries.label: Neanderthals render bone grease at Neumark-Nord, about 125,000 years ago
entries.hint: At Neumark-Nord 2 in central Germany, beside a lake in an interglacial about as warm as today, Neanderthals crushed the bones of at least 172 large mammals — horses, deer, aurochs — into tens of thousands of fragments and heated them in water to render bone grease. A 2025 study calls it the earliest clear case of intensive grease rendering in the Palaeolithic: signs of such intensification had been thought to begin at Upper Palaeolithic sites about 28,000 years ago, long after Neanderthals had gone. More than 16,500 flint artefacts and traces of fire mark a place that was organised and returned to.
entries.note: SECONDARY (university press releases and popular coverage of one paper, found by web search; the paper not read): Kindler et al., Science Advances (2025), on Neumark-Nord 2. The ‘fat factory’ framing and the idea that grease offset a protein-heavy diet are interpretations in the coverage, not findings. Compare fats-8000bc-1200bc::te1, which holds only Kiple’s undated remark that rendering was the first extraction method.

entries.label: Stone lamps burn animal fat: Lascaux and the Upper Palaeolithic
entries.loc: Dordogne, France, and other Palaeolithic caves
entries.hint: The French Ministry of Culture’s account of Lascaux counts over a hundred lamps in the cave, most of them limestone plates with a hollow centre to hold the fuel, and one red sandstone lamp with a handle and an engraving. Analysis of samples from some lamps identified fatty acids of animal origin, and the wicks were conifer and non-woody. Not every ‘lamp’ was one: of 302 artefacts examined in one study only 85 were confirmed as lamps, and burn marks are rare before the Magdalenian. An experiment of 1981 found that animal fat sets hard again when the lamp is out, which suits a portable light.
entries.note: SECONDARY (French Ministry of Culture Lascaux page, a 2002 Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française article and an experimental study of 1981, seen through a web search; not read in full): the 40,000-year start comes from a hobbyist page citing de Beaune & White 1993 and is the loosest part of the bracket; the confirmed-lamp count is de Beaune 1987 as a Spanish cave paper reports it.
